info.bio:
Billy Paul nacido como Paul Williams el 1 de diciembre de 1934 en Philadelphia, Estados Unidos es un músico y cantante de música soul.

Billy Paul comenzó su carrera musical a los 12 años apareciendo en emisoras de radio locales de Philadelphia. Escuchando discos que su madre compraba desarrolló un estilo vocal con raíces en el jazz, el R&B y el pop.

Paul asistió a la Escuela de Música de West Philadelphia para completar su formación en técnica vocal.

scenes.name: Sweet funk: el soul sexual
scenes.book: Funk: The Music, the People, and the Rhythm of the One
scenes.author: Rickey Vincent
scenes.desc: Tras Let’s Get It On, «Me and Mrs. Jones» de Billy Paul y «Let’s Stay Together» de Al Green llegó una nueva hornada de cantantes sensuales. Barry White, con su orquesta de estudio sobre una sección rítmica de R&B, unió la elegancia occidental y la sensualidad negra: un lujo negro impensable diez años antes. Los Moments («Sexy Mama»), Main Ingredient, los Miracles («Do It Baby»), Leon Haywood («I Want’a Do Something Freaky to You», base de «Nothin’ but a G Thang» de Dr. Dre) o New Birth mezclaron psicodelia, melodía y funk sucio; Sylvia Robinson susurró «Pillow Talk» (1973) y Major Harris remató «Love Won’t Let Me Wait» con un orgasmo simulado.

scenes.name: El sonido de Filadelfia
scenes.book: Funk: The Music, the People, and the Rhythm of the One
scenes.author: Rickey Vincent
scenes.desc: El imperio de Kenny Gamble y Leon Huff, distribuido por CBS: los O’Jays, los Intruders, Billy Paul y Harold Melvin & the Blue Notes con Teddy Pendergrass, sobre la banda de la casa MFSB (Norman Harris, Bobby Eli, Ronnie Baker, Earl Young), la más exitosa de los setenta; su «TSOP» fue la sintonía de Soul Train. Los O’Jays fueron el altavoz del comentario social de Gamble: «Back Stabbers» (1972), Ship Ahoy (1974) con su travesía en un barco negrero, «For the Love of Money» (que el éxito convirtió en música de centro comercial), Survival, Family Reunion. Después de 1976 desapareció el mensaje del soul, y con Gloria Gaynor y Donna Summer la frontera entre el disco, el funk y el soul se borró.

podcast.title: "Gray Eyed" Philly Soul
podcast.body: In 1978, Billy Paul characterized Philadelphia soul as "gray eyed," implying that it was, and always had been, a racially integrated musical form, appealing across diverse audiences despite some songs specifically targeting Black communities. "Paul said in 1978 that at that all Philadelphia soul is what he called gray eyed meaning racially integrated and it always has been."

podcast.title: Criticism of "Am I Black Enough for You" Release
podcast.body: Billy Paul openly blamed Kenny Gamble and Clive Davis for releasing "Am I Black Enough for You" as the successor to his international hit "Me and Mrs. Jones," contending that its explicitly targeted appeal to Black audiences limited its commercial reach and consequently hindered his subsequent career. "Billy Paul blamed Gamble and Clive Davis for releasing a song that he said had, quote, limited appeal."

srcs.episode: Ep. 37 - Philly Soul and the Sound of the 70s

podcast.title: Jazz Background
podcast.body: Billy Paul primarily identified as a jazz singer, having performed with the legendary Dinah Washington as a child and jammed with Charlie Parker, a background that initially made him reluctant to record the pop-oriented "Me and Mrs. Jones." "Paul was a jazz singer and wondered why he was being given a pop song This was a guy who sang with the great Dino Washington when he was a child, he had jammed with the bird Charlie Parker and he was supposed to sing a pop song about a couple of people having an affair"

srcs.episode: Ep. 37 - Philly Soul and the Sound of the 70s

podcast.title: Personal Connection to "Me and Mrs. Jones"
podcast.body: Billy Paul's decision to record the pop song "Me and Mrs. Jones" was influenced by his own marital difficulties, as he felt a personal connection to the song's narrative of an extramarital affair, which he believed he could authentically convey. "he was having some marital problems and well, he had his own Mrs. Jones, he thought maybe he could relate and well, he sure sang as if he could"
